text.en: Two outdoorsmen in northern British Columbia's remote Kakwa Provincial Park chanced on a remarkable find: thousands of dinosaur footprints scattered across a cliff. The dinosaur stomping ground was trampled by theropods, ornithopods, and Tetrapodosaurus back in the Cretaceous, then preserved in stone, only to be discovered some 140 million years later.

details.notes: Map of British Columbia with Kakwa Provincial Park marked. Photo at bottom left captioned 'Prince George, BC, 2000' shows Garnet Fraser, described as amateur paleontologist and general physician in Prince George, BC. His friend Bryan Monroe first spotted the tracks back in 2000. Illustration of a theropod dinosaur alongside cast. S001 label visible at bottom right.

text.en: Algae in our oceans, like the tropical rainforests, maintain about one-fifth of the world's oxygen supply. They turn sunlight, carbon dioxide into sugars and oxygen for other organisms to eat and breathe, and they provide important habitat for marine organisms.

text.en: Millions of coralline algae, ranging from flat crusts to finely branched forms, live on Vancouver Island's rocky shores. Coralline algae don't grow near Vancouver because our sea water is not salty enough: it's diluted by the Fraser River.

details.notes: Six coralline algae specimens displayed, all collected from Botanical Beach, BC in July 2010. S036 label visible at bottom right.

text.en: Christmas fern is green all year round, even at Christmas. In winter, its fronds don't brown and wither like those of most other ferns, they just lay flat to the ground. Next year's growth comes up tall and green in spring.

text.en: Every piece of hard or soft coral, from tropical reef-builders to cold-water dwellers, is a community of tiny polyps, related to anemones. Most tropical coral polyps harbour microscopic algae called zooxanthellae 'zo-zan-thell-ee,' which convert sunlight into nutrients that help corals form hard skeletons. Cold-water corals often survive without them.

text.en: Tropical corals need coastal mangrove forests. Mangroves clean water flowing from the land, and nearby seagrass beds provide nursery habitat for baby fish, invertebrate animals, and other reef life. When mangroves are destroyed by coastal development, marine life suffers and corals die from cloudy, polluted waters. One-third of all corals and the animals that depend on them are endangered.

text.en: What do you see in this drawer: fruits or vegetables? If you said fruits, you think like a botanist -- a scientist who studies plants. Fruits contain the seeds of flowering plants. This means many culinary vegetables, such as tomatoes, bean pods, okra, eggplants, peppers, and squash, are technically fruits.

text.en: These "flowers" are not flowers at all. The white petals of Pacific dogwood are actually modified leaves, called bracts, encircling 30 to 40 small green flowers. The big white "petals" attract pollinators to the tiny real flowers.

details.notes: Inset diagram labels: "Flowerhead with small, dense, individual flowers." Bottom-left label: Pacific dogwood / Cornus nuttallii / May 4, 2011 / Point Roberts, Washington / No. E.0003. Decorative line drawings of dogwood flowers in background.

text.en: If you discover and describe a new species, you can give it a name. Whenever we refer to the species, even if centuries from now, we would use this name and remember that you described it. Most species of fungi are undescribed—there may be one awaiting discovery in your backyard! R.J. Bandoni and M. Zang described and named this fungus, so we refer to it as Tremella aurantialba Bandoni & Zang.

text.en: Graptolites are extinct filter-feeding animals that lived from 500 to 350 million years ago. They lived as colonies, their small, soft bodies protected by a common skeleton. Most graptolite fossils show the skeleton flattened like a pancake, preserved as a ghostly carbon film on the rocks. This is what graptolite colonies might have looked like in life.

text.en: Underfoot in Vancouver's parks and ravines people have found fossils of ferns, conifers, flowering plants, and shells, some of which date as far back as 55 million years. The fossils you see here were found in Vancouver's neighbourhood of Kitsilano.
